Here's the market in October twenty twenty-six. Output is five times input in eight of these ten rows, and never less. But the cheapest input, ten cents a million, is a hundredth of the priciest, ten dollars. So the model you pick usually moves the bill more than any prompt trick. And half these rows hide a length threshold. Past two hundred seventy-two thousand tokens on GPT six, the whole request pays double for its input. So on Sol, a three-hundred-thousand-token prompt costs a dollar twenty to send, not sixty cents. That's the price sheet. Now, what does a real workload cost?

Take one support-bot request: twelve hundred tokens in, three hundred out. On Sonnet, that's about half a cent. Basically nothing. Now serve a hundred thousand of them. Twenty-seven dollars on Haiku, twenty-seven hundred on Fable. Same task, same tokens, a hundred times apart.

Conversations are where estimates go wrong. The model keeps no memory between turns, so every turn resends the whole chat so far. The new message is a thin slice on top of everything you've already paid for. On Sonnet, ten turns cost thirteen cents. Twenty, thirty-seven and a half. Forty, a dollar nineteen. Double the turns, and the bill roughly triples.

Thinking tokens are the other surprise. They're billed as output. Keep the request and its four-hundred-token answer the same. Add eight thousand thinking tokens, and it costs eleven times as much. Twenty thousand, twenty-six times. And the answer you see never got any longer.
